title: Ploy's ticket booth: which price wins?

story.place: the ticket booth of a small cinema in Chiang Mai
story.text: Ploy sells tickets at a small cinema. Children under 12 pay 80 baht, students pay 120, everyone else pays 180. Yesterday a 9-year-old with a student card was charged the wrong price, and her dad wants to know why.

steps.name: A puzzled parent
steps.text: The booth script decides the price with if, elif and else. First we run it for a 15-year-old student.

steps.name: The first question
steps.text: Python reaches line 3 and asks its question.

predict.question: With age 15, is `age < 12` True or False?
predict.reveal: False. 15 is not less than 12, so line 4 is skipped.

steps.name: The second question
steps.text: Because the first answer was False, Python moves to the elif.

predict.question: Which price is printed for this customer?
predict.reveal: 120. is_student is True, so the elif branch runs.

predict.question: Does the line `price = 180` run for this customer?
predict.reveal: No. Once one branch has run, Python skips the rest of the chain, else included.

verify.code:
age = 15
is_student = True
ran = "No"
if age < 12:
    price = 80
elif is_student:
    price = 120
else:
    price = 180
    ran = "Yes"
print(ran)

steps.name: A 9-year-old student
steps.text: Same script, but now the customer is 9 and has a student card.

predict.question: What price is printed now?
predict.reveal: 80. The first condition is True now, so Python never even checks the elif.

steps.what_changed: age 15 -> 9: the first condition becomes True, price 120 -> 80; the elif is not checked.

steps.name: Swap the two checks
steps.text: A colleague moved the student check to the top. Same 9-year-old student.

predict.question: What price is printed with the checks swapped?
predict.reveal: 120. The student check is first and it is True, so Python stops there. That is yesterday's bug.

steps.what_changed: order swapped: the same child pays 120 instead of 80, because the first True condition wins.

steps.name: An adult without a card
steps.text: Back to the original order. Now the customer is 30 and not a student.

predict.question: What price is printed?
predict.reveal: 180. Both questions were False, so the else branch runs.

steps.name: Recap
steps.text: How Python picks one branch, in three sentences.

recap: Python checks the if, then each elif, top to bottom, and runs only the first branch whose condition is True.
else runs only when none of the conditions above it were True.
So the order of the checks is part of the rule: put the most specific case first.

apply.prompt: Fern's weather app shows one word for the day. Write a program that reads a temperature (a whole number) and prints `cold` below 15, `nice` from 15 to 28, and `hot` above 28.
apply.starter_code:
temperature = int(input())
# print cold, nice or hot

must_fail.why: two separate ifs: 10 prints cold and nice

hints.text: How many words should the program print for one temperature? Which keyword makes Python pick only one branch?
Test your edges: what should 15 print, and what should 28 print? Check that each comparison includes or excludes the right end.
Similar shape for a grade: `if score < 50: print('retry')`, then `elif score <= 79: print('pass')`, then `else: print('merit')`. One chain, first True wins. Build your temperature chain the same way.

explain.prompt: Ploy's colleague swapped the two checks, and a 9-year-old student was charged 120 instead of 80. Explain why changing the order changed the price.

criteria.text: Says the conditions are checked from top to bottom.
Says only the first branch whose condition is True runs; the rest are skipped.
Applies it: with the student check first, it is True for the child, so the age check is never reached.

grader.reference_answer: Python asks the questions in order and stops at the first True one. With the student check on top, the 9-year-old's student card makes it True, so 120 is chosen and the under-12 check never runs.

hints.text: In what order does Python ask the questions in an if/elif chain?
For the 9-year-old student, which condition is True first in the swapped version? What happens to the ones after it?
Guided example in another setting: a lift that asks 'is it the top floor?' before 'is the door blocked?' never notices the blocked door on the top floor. Use the same idea for Ploy's two checks.

transfer.prompt: An online shop charges delivery: free for orders of 1000 baht or more, 30 baht from 500 to 999, and 60 baht below 500. A customer with a 1200 baht order was charged 30. Fix the program.

must_fail.code:
total = int(input())
fee = 60
if total >= 1000:
    fee = 0
if total >= 500:
    fee = 30
print(fee)
must_fail.why: separate ifs: the second one overwrites free delivery

hints.text: Run it in your head with 1200. Which condition is checked first, and is it True?
Once the first condition is True, Python never looks at the elif. Which question should come first so 1200 can reach free delivery?
Similar: a gym gives 'gold' at 100 visits and 'silver' at 50. Checking `>= 50` first means 120 visits only gets silver; asking about 100 first fixes it. Look at the order of your two checks.
x is 7. Which condition is the first one that is True?
After a branch runs, does Python look at the remaining elif and else?
Similar: with `n = 10`, `if n > 0: print('pos')` then `elif n > 5: print('ten-ish')` prints only pos, even though both are True. Then the line after the chain runs.
